title: People Have Counted So Many Verses as Abrogated
intro: In a chapter of al-Itqan, al-Suyuti examines verses said to contain a ruling superseded by a later one. He then puts the cases into ten lines of verse. A single word such as “steadfastness” or “alliance” can stand for a whole passage he has just discussed. His tally includes disputed cases, and the closing line records two further proposals whose rulings he believes still stand.

translation: People have counted so many verses as abrogated
and included more than can be numbered.
1.sharh: Older lists kept growing because their authors sometimes counted a rule as repealed when a later passage only narrowed its scope. Al-Suyuti wants to know which earlier rulings actually ceased to apply.

translation: Here is a list of verses, with nothing to add,
twenty that skilled and eminent scholars have sifted.
2.sharh: “Twenty” is the result of sifting earlier claims. Al-Suyuti explains in prose that he reaches that number by including the verse on the direction of prayer under one interpretation of it.

translation: The verses on where to turn, wherever one may be, and the duty
of the dying to make a bequest to their family,
3.sharh: On a reading attributed to Ibn Abbas, the instruction to face the Kaaba (2:144) superseded the freedom to turn in any direction (2:115). The second case concerns the obligation to make a bequest to parents and relatives (2:180) when inheritance shares were later prescribed.

translation: the ban on eating after sleep and on intercourse,
and the well-known payment in lieu for those able to fast,
4.sharh: These are nights in Ramadan. An early restriction applied once a person had slept, even though dawn had yet to break. The second example concerns the former choice, on one reading of 2:184–185, to feed someone in need in place of fasting.

translation: fearing Him as He is due, according to an authentic report,
and fighting unbelievers in the sacred month,
5.sharh: The question is how “as He is due” (3:102) relates to “as much as you can” (64:16). Some read the second as relief from the first obligation, others as a statement of its meaning. The other example is the dispute over the sacred months in 2:217 and 5:2.

translation: a widow’s year of waiting and the bequest for her,
and the reckoning for inward speech and thoughts,
6.sharh: Al-Suyuti distinguishes the widow’s waiting period, set at four months and ten days in 2:234, from provision for her in 2:240. He then pairs the account of hidden thoughts (2:284) with the assurance that God asks of a soul only what it can bear (2:286).

translation: the sworn alliance, confinement for illicit sex, declining to judge
unbelievers’ cases, calling them as witnesses, standing firm, marching out,
7.sharh: The six cues concern inheritance by sworn alliance (4:33), confinement (4:15), a judge’s choice to decline a case (5:42), witnesses to a will on a journey (5:106), steadfastness in battle (8:65–66) and who was called to go out (9:41, 122).

translation: the marriage restriction on a man or woman guilty of illicit sex,
and the marriages forbidden to the Chosen One,
8.sharh: The first question is whether the marriage restriction in 24:3 remained in force alongside the direction to marry off the unmarried (24:32). The second concerns the restriction on further marriages addressed specifically to the Prophet in 33:52.

translation: the bridal payment for a woman who came over, the verse on
speaking with him privately, and the night vigil set down in writing.
9.sharh: The first phrase recalls the repayment of bridal gifts when spouses were separated by migration (60:10–11). The next refers to giving alms before a private audience with the Prophet (58:12–13), the last to the easing of the night vigil (73:2, 20).

translation: Some add the verse on those in bondage asking leave to enter,
and the gift for those present when an estate is divided.
10.sharh: Some added household privacy at three times of day (24:58) and a gift for relatives, orphans and needy people present when an estate is divided (4:8). In his prose al-Suyuti judges both rulings to be in force, however often people neglect them.

1.1.5.head: المَنسوخ
1.1.5.meaning: Mansukh, a ruling understood to have been superseded by later revelation. The verses listed here continue to be recited.

2.1.1.head: هاكَ
2.1.1.meaning: “Here, take it.” The poet hands the reader the result of his inquiry.

2.1.2.head: تَحرير
2.1.2.meaning: Careful examination that identifies the precise matter at issue.

2.2.3.head: الحُذّاق
2.2.3.meaning: Those skilled in a discipline and able to judge a disputed point.

3.1.2.head: التَّوَجُّه
3.1.2.meaning: Facing a direction in prayer. The question concerns the prescribed direction, the qibla.

3.2.1.head: أَوصى
3.2.1.meaning: To make a bequest that takes effect after the giver’s death.

3.2.2.head: أَهل
3.2.2.meaning: His family. Ibn Aqila gives the shorter form heard here. Al-Suyuti’s al-Itqan and the verse card have li-ahlīhi (لأهليه), with a long ī. Both refer to a bequest to relatives.

4.1.6.head: رَفَث
4.1.6.meaning: Sexual intercourse, the sense of the word in the verse about nights in Ramadan.

4.2.1.head: فِديَة
4.2.1.meaning: Fidya, a payment in lieu. Here it is food for someone in need in place of a day’s fast.

4.2.2.head: مُطيق
4.2.2.meaning: Someone capable of the act. The ability to fast is precisely what matters in this dispute.

5.1.6.head: أَثَر
5.1.6.meaning: Athar, a transmitted report from an earlier authority, here about the interpretation of a verse.

5.2.4.head: الأُلى
5.2.4.meaning: An early relative pronoun meaning “those who”.

6.1.1.head: الاِعتِداد
6.1.1.meaning: Observing the prescribed waiting period, here after a husband’s death.

6.1.2.head: حَول
6.1.2.meaning: One full year, the period in Quran 2:240.

6.2.2.head: دينَ
6.2.2.meaning: To be called to account. What passes through the mind is made the grammatical subject.

7.1.1.head: الحِلف
7.1.1.meaning: A sworn alliance that could once give one party a share in the other’s estate.

7.1.4-5.head: تَرَكَ
7.1.4-5.meaning: “Leaving those who disbelieve”: the phrase continues into the next half. It refers to declining to hear a case brought before the Prophet.

7.2.2.head: إِشهاد
7.2.2.meaning: Calling witnesses, here non-Muslims witnessing a traveller’s will.

7.2.4.head: النَّفَر
7.2.4.meaning: Going forth in answer to a general summons, as in sura 9.

8.1.2.head: عَقد
8.1.2.meaning: The marriage contract. The legal transaction stands for marriage in this line.

8.2.3.meaning: Al-Mustafa, the Chosen One, a title of the Prophet Muhammad.

8.2.6.head: مُحتَظَر
8.2.6.meaning: Barred or forbidden. The root can mean fencing something off. The nearby sound muhtadir in the third verse has a different consonant and means a dying person.

9.1.2.head: مَهر
9.1.2.meaning: Mahr, the bridal gift owed to the wife. Here payments already made are being settled after migration.

9.1.6.head: نَجوى
9.1.6.meaning: Najwa, private conversation. The word runs across the verse break and its pronoun refers to the Prophet.

9.2.5.head: مُستَطَر
9.2.5.meaning: Set down in writing, here recorded in scripture.

10.1.5.head: مَلَكَ
10.1.5.meaning: An allusion to the Quranic expression for enslaved members of a household in 24:58.

10.2.2.head: القِسمَة
10.2.2.meaning: The division of an estate. The verse concerns people who attend without holding an heir’s share.
